newsitem.title: GERMANY: JOBS-Foreigners - friend or foe of EU worker?.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Foreigners - friend or foe of EU worker?.

text.p: When West Germany was rebuilding from the rubble of World War II, it invited millions of "guest workers" from countries such as Turkey, Italy and Yugoslavia to help in the creation of its economic miracle.
But now the miracle is over.
Massive unemployment, hitting post-war records, has sparked a heated debate on whether the "guests" have outstayed their welcome in the labour market of a united Germany.

"We have the problem of high unemployment among Germans but at the same time we employ many foreigners," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in January. "It should be legitimate to look at ways to make sure Germans get the jobs."
German unemployment stood at a seasonally adjusted 4.316 million in February -- a joblessness rate of 11.3 percent.

Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), the arch-conservative Bavarian party which forms part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's governing coalition, wants to impose tougher restrictions on work permits for foreigners from outside the European Union.
The party also wants legislation to force Germans to take jobs which at the moment only foreigners are prepared to accept.
Critics accuse the CSU of whipping up racist sentiment and insist foreign labour is not a major cause of the highest German unemployment since Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933.
DEBATE REVERBERATES ACROSS EUROPE
The latest statistics from Germany's Federal Labour Office indicate around 2.1 million foreign workers are registered in Germany and paying social security.

Around 600,000 Turks form the largest part of this group, followed by around 420,000 from the former Yugoslavia and then Italians, Greeks and Spaniards. The number of foreigners working illegally can only be guessed at.
But the debate is not restricted to Germany. The old argument of blaming foreign workers for "taking away" jobs appears to have resurfaced with a vengeance amid Europe's unemployment crisis.

The extreme-right National Front has won control of several towns in southern France by campaigning strongly on the issue of immigration and its leader Jean-Marie Le Pen won 15 percent of the national vote in the 1995 presidential election.
In Austria, where unemployment has also climbed to the highest level in the country's post-war history, far right leader Joerg Haider has called for foreigners to be repatriated.
A regional branch of his Freedom Party provoked outrage last month when it declared that public building contracts should only go to firms which do not employ foreign workers.
But, in Germany at least, it is not just the conservatives who want action against foreign workers.
BUILDING SITE AS BATTLEGROUND

A walk around Berlin, currently Europe's biggest building site as the city races to prepare for the government's move from Bonn by the end of the decade, points up the sector in which resentment of foreign workers can be especially high.
The banter of the building workers is often more likely to be in Portuguese, Polish or English -- sometimes with an Irish accent -- than in German.
The construction sector trade union IG Bau estimates around 400,000 foreign workers are undercutting their German counterparts on building sites across the country.
Constructors "sub contract" work to foreign firms which are in reality no more than workers willing to declare themselves "self-employed" to avoid social security contributions.

"When a contract is given to a company from Portugal, for example, they're not really working as a company here at all," IG Bau spokesman Werner Koehler told Reuters. "They're just sending over cheap workers."

IG Bau is as angry at foreign workers from within the European Union exploiting legal loopholes as it is at those from the likes of eastern Europe who flooded in after the fall of the Berlin Wall and who work illegally.
After much wringing of hands, employers and unions agreed a minimum wage in the construction sector which came into force at the beginning of the year as a first step to combat the problem.
"We can't really judge the effect of the new law yet because there's not much building work going on in the current weather," Koehler said.
"But the only way to really crack down on these people and these firms is to increase controls, to have more raids on building sites."
CONTROVERSIAL CONCLUSIONS
But critics say the case against foreign workers is not just morally wrong -- it is also statistically flawed.
Bernhard Jagoda, the president of the Federal Labour Office, said on Thursday after announcing the latest jobless figures that the argument was "total nonsense".
A working group from the opposition Social Democrats said in a study last year that although 1.37 million work permits were issued in Germany 1995, this tells little of the real story.

It pointed out that in around 950,000 cases, the permits could only be issued if no "preferred employees" -- a phrase which above all means Germans or members of EU states -- were available to do the jobs.

After further calculations, the experts concluded additional work permit restrictions could realistically only be applied to around 100,000-150,000 full-time jobs, if Germany was prepared to suffer the damage to its international image.
And even then, it was more likely employers would re-employ the foreigners illegally rather than take on German workers.

"The sad conclusion must be that a more restrictive practice of issuing work permits would lead to the foreigners affected being employed illegally -- probably with far worse working conditions than they have at the moment," the group said.
